pronunciation.approximation: aw-bah-TAH-LAH — low on 'aw-bah', then high on 'TAH-LAH'.

kin.label: Yoruba etymology
kin.form: Ọbàtálá, from ọba 'king' + ti 'of' + alá 'white cloth' — 'King of the White Cloth' (Abraham, Dictionary of Modern Yoruba; Idowu, Olódùmarè)

kin.label: Alternate name
kin.form: Ọ̀rìṣànlá / Orishanla, 'the great orisha' — his title in the oldest strata of the Ifá corpus (Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief)

kin.label: Brazilian Portuguese
kin.form: Oxalá, the phonetic adaptation of Ọbàtálá carried across the Atlantic; highest of the orixás in Candomblé (Verger, Orixás)

pronunciation.note: Ọbàtálá is Tier 1: the dot below ọ and the acute accents on the final two syllables are distinctive features the ASCII form loses, the acutes preserving high tones. The dot below ọ marks the open [ɔ] vowel, a phonemic distinction essential to Yoruba.

domains.title: King of the White Cloth
domains.subtitle: Creation, Purity, and Peaceful Judgment
domains.lead:
Ọbàtálá is the orixá who shapes humanity. While Olódùmarè breathes the soul into the body, Ọbàtálá is the sculptor who moulds the limbs, the one whose hands first pressed cool clay into human form. He is the eldest of the orishas in many accounts, the patron of white cloth, purity, peace, and the aged. His voice is soft, his judgments slow, and his anger terrible precisely because it is so rare.

He is also the guardian of those whom the world calls imperfect: the disabled, the deformed, the albino. In Yoruba thought, these are not mistakes; they are Ọbàtálá's own children, marked by his hand.

cards.name: Creator of Bodies
cards.desc: He moulds human form from earth; Olódùmarè alone gives it breath.

cards.name: White Cloth
cards.desc: Spotless garments, white beads, and cool water mark his altars and his devotees.

cards.name: Peaceful Judgment
cards.desc: He settles disputes with patience; his curses fall on the unjustly proud.

cards.name: Patron of the Vulnerable
cards.desc: The disabled and the elderly are his special children; harming them offends him directly.

symbols.name: White cloth
symbols.meaning: Purity, coolness, and the veil between the human and the divine.

symbols.name: Snail shell
symbols.meaning: The slow, deliberate pace of Ọbàtálá's wisdom and the spiral of creation.

symbols.name: Ivory or white bead necklace
symbols.meaning: His sacred colour and the wealth of patience.

symbols.name: Calabash of cool water
symbols.meaning: Coolness of temperament; the antidote to hot anger.

mythology.lead: Ọbàtálá's mythology turns on creation, sobriety, and the cost of pride — preserved in the corpus of Ifá divination poetry (odu), in the oral histories of Ilé-Ifẹ̀, and, across the Atlantic, in the liturgies of Candomblé and Santería, where the details shift with each retelling. He is the elder who knows that making life is more difficult than destroying it.

myths.title: The Moulding of Humanity
myths.text: When Olódùmarè, the supreme God, resolved to people the earth, Ọbàtálá — also known as Ọ̀rìṣànlá, 'the great orisha' — took up the making of bodies. From clay given him by Olódùmarè he moulded each human form with care, and Olódùmarè breathed the emí, the living soul, into what his servant's hands had shaped. But one day, working, Ọbàtálá drank too much palm wine, and the figures he shaped that afternoon came out twisted, incomplete, unfinished. Olódùmarè gave them life anyway, and they remain among us — the disabled, the albino, the differently formed. From that day Ọbàtálá forbade palm wine to all who serve him and took these children of the drunken afternoon as his own, to be honored and never mocked. The myth is told across the Ifá corpus and the diaspora; its point is exact — even the maker's failure is gathered into the design, and the people the world calls broken are the ones heaven claims first.

myths.title: The Contest for Ilé-Ifẹ̀
myths.text: Yoruba cosmogony tells that Olódùmarè once charged the orishas with creating solid earth from the primordial waters, giving them a chain, a hen, and a bag of sand for the work. The mission fell to Ọbàtálá, who climbed down the chain — but paused on the way, drank palm wine, fell into sleep, and dropped the bag of sand. Odùduwà, coming after, caught it, scattered the sand upon the waters, and set the hen to scratching: where the hen scratched, the first dry land rose, and on it Odùduwà founded Ilé-Ifẹ̀, the city of origin from which the Yoruba kingdoms descend. The sources disagree on details — some traditions name Ọbàtálá as the intended creator, others give the mission to Odùduwà from the first — and the rivalry between elder orisha and founding king became a standing theme of Ifá poetry. The myth encodes history as well as theology: Ifẹ̀'s supremacy is not brute primacy but a succession debated, remembered, and argued over in verse for a thousand years.

myths.title: The Elder of the Orishas
myths.text: In many odu of Ifá, Ọbàtálá is the eldest of the orishas, the one who remembers the beginning of things. He takes no part in the thunder and river-drama of the younger powers; his authority rests on age, whiteness, and the fact that every human body was once clay in his hands. When kings fail and war-gods have exhausted themselves, the Ifá verses send the supplicant to Ọbàtálá — the orisha of the second chance, consulted when force has failed and only patience remains. His priesthood keeps among the strictest disciplines in Yoruba religion: white cloth, cool water, no palm wine, no raised voice. The mythology's quiet argument is that in a pantheon of spectacular powers, the eldest power is the unspectacular one — clarity, slowness, and the refusal to be provoked, worn like white cloth in a loud world.

myths.title: The Curse of Pride
myths.text: Ọbàtálá's stories turn on arrogance and its correction. In one widely told narrative, a man mocked a cripple in the marketplace; Ọbàtálá, whose children the mocker had laughed at, afflicted him with confusion until he crawled to the orisha's shrine to beg pardon. In others the proud lose their speech or find their limbs frozen mid-gesture until restitution is made. The punishment always fits the offense with uncomfortable precision: those who mocked the imperfect are made imperfect; those who despised the slow are halted. His justice is cool, deliberate, and inescapable — the mythic face of the Yoruba ideal of ìtẹ̀lọ́rùn, the patient, cool heart, which counts calm as strength and impatience as a disease of character. The myth is a warning aimed at the able-bodied: the body's completeness is a loan, not a possession.

myths.title: Oxalá Crosses the Atlantic
myths.text: Carried across the Atlantic in the holds of slave ships, Ọbàtálá was reborn as Oxalá, the white-clad father of the Candomblé nations of Brazil, and as Obatalá of Cuban Santería. In diaspora cosmogony the creation story is retold with new economy: Oxalá descends to make the world, pauses to rest — and wakes to find the work done, or done wrongly, by another orisha; his white garments become the first light. Brazilian liturgy divides him into two paths of one power: the aged, endlessly patient Oxalá and the youthful, quick-tempered Oxaguiã. Cuban houses honor Obatalá with white beads and cool water on quiet altars, syncretised in Catholic imagery with the white-robed Christ. The myth's endurance across the Middle Passage is itself its meaning: a god of gentle hands survived the century that tried to break every hand that carried him.

lore.syncretism: In Brazilian Candomblé, Ọbàtálá became Oxalá, often syncretised with Jesus Christ in his role as the white-robed saviour and with the dove as a symbol of peace. In Cuban Santería he remains Obatalá, father of the white beads, and is divided into youthful and aged paths (Obatalá Ayáguna and Obatalá Orishánlá; Oxaguiã and Oxalufã in Brazil). The Catholic overlay preserved his colour and gentleness while translating his mythology into a Christian idiom of purity and creation. In Africa itself, Ọbàtálá stands in a studied complementarity with the thunder-god Ṣàngó and the ferocious Ògún: where they are hot, he is cool; where they cut, he binds. The orishas function less as rivals than as a single temperament distributed across many bodies, and Ọbàtálá holds the body's share.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ọbàtálá's influence extends far beyond formal religion. The Yoruba value of ìtẹ̀lọ́rùn — patience, coolness of heart — is modelled on his temperament. In the African diaspora his white garments appear in Candomblé, Santería (Lukumí), and Trinidad Orisha; the feast days of Oxalá are among the most important in the Bahian ritual year. Artists and disability-rights advocates have reclaimed him as a divine patron of bodily difference, while environmental thinkers see in his clay-and-breath creation story an early recognition that matter and spirit are not separate. Every white garment worn at a Candomblé ceremony is his signature still.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ọbàtálá is the god of the second look. The first glance sees deformity, age, weakness, or strangeness; the second glance, his glance, sees the hand of the maker. He asks us to slow down — to judge slowly, to speak softly, to remember that every body was once unformed clay.

In a culture obsessed with speed and perfection, Ọbàtálá's white cloth is a radical statement. It says that purity is not the absence of flaw but the presence of care. His palm-wine story is not a moral about alcohol; it is a moral about consequence. Even the maker of bodies can mar what he makes. The question is not whether we are perfect, but whether we treat the imperfect with the reverence due to the creator's own work.

lore.archaeology: No temple of Ọbàtálá has been excavated as such; his archaeology is embedded in the urban fabric of Ilé-Ifẹ̀, where excavations in the twentieth century uncovered shrine deposits and the naturalistic terracotta and bronze heads of the twelfth–fifteenth centuries — the art of the city he is credited with founding. What does not survive is the perishable core of his cult: white cloth, offerings of cool water, and palm-wine libations leave no trace in the Yoruba soil. Across the Atlantic, the material record is richer — his white bead necklaces, snail shells, ivory bracelets, and calabashes are conserved in collections of Afro-Brazilian religion in São Paulo and Salvador and in the museums of Afro-Cuban religion in Havana and Matanzas — while the Ifá corpus itself, recited by diviners to this day, preserves the creation narrative in an unbroken oral line older than any of them.
